clinicalPearls: Factor H is the principal fluid-phase regulator of the alternative complement pathway; loss of function permits uncontrolled C3 turnover and consumption
Complete (homozygous) deficiency produces a low C3 with a normal C4 pattern and predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infection, particularly invasive meningococcal disease
Heterozygous variants and an acquired anti-factor H autoantibody form (frequently accompanied by CFHR1/CFHR3 deletion) are strongly linked to atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Factor H abnormalities are also central to C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis), where alternative pathway dysregulation drives glomerular C3 deposition

The functionally important surface-regulatory defects cluster in the C-terminal domains that mediate recognition of host endothelium and glomerular basement membrane, explaining organ-specific injury despite systemic complement activation
A common CFH polymorphism (Y402H) is a major genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, illustrating roles for the gene beyond infection
It is important to separate the complete deficiency (infection phenotype) from partial or surface-specific regulatory defects that present as thrombotic microangiopathy or glomerulopathy
Meningococcal and other encapsulated-organism vaccination, together with prompt treatment of febrile illness, is central to reducing infective risk
reference.pathophysiology: Factor H, encoded by CFH within the regulators-of-complement-activation gene cluster, is a plasma glycoprotein that restrains the alternative pathway amplification loop. Its amino-terminal short consensus repeats give it its regulatory activity: it acts as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and accelerates the irreversible decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). Its carboxy-terminal repeats bind polyanions and surface-bound C3b, allowing the protein to discriminate host surfaces from activating ones. Complete deficiency abolishes fluid-phase control, so continuous alternative pathway tick-over consumes C3 and factor B and leaves circulating C3 persistently low; the resulting failure to opsonise encapsulated organisms and to generate membrane attack complex underlies susceptibility to infection. In contrast, defects that selectively impair surface regulation, whether C-terminal variants or blocking autoantibodies, leave fluid-phase C3 relatively preserved but expose the glomerular and endothelial surfaces to unchecked complement attack, producing atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or C3 glomerulopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other alternative pathway regulator defects (factor I, membrane cofactor protein/CD46, thrombomodulin)
Gain-of-function variants of C3 or factor B causing complement overactivation
Other early or terminal complement component deficiencies presenting with neisserial infection
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies
Immune complex and post-infectious glomerulonephritis for the glomerulopathy presentation
Secondary complement consumption from active systemic lupus erythematosus or sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Complement profile demonstrating low C3 with normal C4 (an alternative pathway pattern)
Factor H antigenic level together with a functional assay
CFH gene sequencing and copy number analysis, including the adjacent CFHR region
Anti-factor H autoantibody testing with CFHR1/CFHR3 deletion analysis
Alternative pathway functional assay (AP50) and terminal pathway assessment
Renal biopsy with complement immunostaining where glomerulopathy or thrombotic microangiopathy is suspected
Blood film for microangiopathic haemolysis with monitoring of renal function
redFlags: Features of invasive meningococcal disease such as fever, non-blanching rash and meningism requiring immediate treatment
Acute kidney injury with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia suggesting atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or nephrotic-range proteinuria
Recurrent thrombotic microangiopathy, including recurrence in a transplanted kidney
reference.prognosis: Complete deficiency carries a lifelong risk of severe encapsulated-organism infection, but this is greatly reduced by vaccination and prompt antibiotic treatment. The atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy phenotypes may progress to kidney failure, although complement-directed therapies have markedly improved outcomes for eligible patients.
pitfalls: Overlooking factor H deficiency when C3 is low but C4 is normal
Assuming a normal factor H antigenic level excludes disease when the defect is functional or surface-specific
Attributing atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome solely to inherited variants and missing the acquired anti-factor H antibody form
Failing to provide encapsulated-organism vaccination and a standby treatment plan for febrile illness
Not anticipating disease recurrence after kidney transplantation in complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome
references: National complement deficiency and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome guidance
management: Prevent infection through immunisation against encapsulated organisms, especially meningococcus, with antibiotic prophylaxis and prompt treatment of febrile illness
Treat atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome with a terminal complement C5 inhibitor such as eculizumab or ravulizumab, supported by plasma exchange or infusion and renal replacement therapy as needed
Cover meningococcal risk before and during C5-inhibitor therapy with vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis
Manage the antibody-mediated form with immunosuppression and plasma exchange to remove the anti-factor H autoantibody
Treat C3 glomerulopathy with complement-directed and immunosuppressive therapy alongside supportive management of proteinuria and renal function
Plan renal transplantation, where kidney failure supervenes, with anti-complement prophylaxis given the high recurrence risk
Provide genetic counselling and family screening, and manage through a nephrology and complement specialist multidisciplinary team
